uncited: Dual Contouring optimizes vertex position via a Quadratic Error Function (QEF) to preserve sharp features [778-dual-contouring.md], while Surface Nets uses a weighted average of intersection points for a faster, normal-free approximation [921-surface-nets.md].
Unlike Marching Cubes, which may produce multiple vertices per cell, these methods produce exactly one vertex per active cell [778-dual-contouring.md][921-surface-nets.md].
**Vertex Placement**: Computing a single 3D position $V$ for each active cell.
* In **Dual Contouring**, $V$ minimizes the error $\|AV - b\|^2$, where rows of $A$ are surface normals and $b_i = n_i \cdot P_i$ [778-dual-contouring.md].
* In **Surface Nets**, $V$ is the centroid of intersection points on the cell edges [921-surface-nets.md].
**Topology Construction**: Connecting the single vertex of each active cell to form the mesh.
Dual Contouring was introduced as an improvement over Marching Cubes to handle sharp features and non-manifold geometries [778-dual-contouring.md].
Surface Nets was proposed as a simplified alternative to Dual Contouring that avoids the computational cost of QEF solving [921-surface-nets.md].
Sparse Dual Marching Cubes extends these concepts to sparse voxel representations [3801-sparse-dual-marching-cubes.md].
